header:
How to choose
a health plan

lines.text: Comparing health plans by premium? That's the wrong number.
lines.say: Comparing health plans by premium? That's the wrong number.

lines.text: The monthly premium is the number everyone looks at, and it hides most of the story.
lines.say: The monthly premium is the number everyone looks at, and it hides most of the story.

lines.text: And the stakes are big. In KFF's 2025 survey, the average employer family plan cost $26,993 a year.
lines.say: And the stakes are big. In K F F's twenty twenty-five survey, the average employer family plan cost almost twenty-seven thousand dollars a year.

lines.text: Workers paid $6,850 of that, on average, before a single doctor visit.
lines.say: Workers paid six thousand eight hundred fifty dollars of that, on average, before a single doctor visit.

lines.text: And that bill keeps growing. The average family premium was $17,545 in 2015.
lines.say: And that bill keeps growing. The average family premium was about seventeen and a half thousand dollars in twenty fifteen.

lines.text: By 2025 it was 54% higher, which is why one fall decision matters so much.
lines.say: By twenty twenty-five it was fifty-four percent higher, which is why one fall decision matters so much.

lines.text: So in this guide, we'll pick a plan the way an actuary would, in four steps, with real math.
lines.say: So in this guide, we'll pick a plan the way an actuary would, in four steps, with real math.

lines.text: No jargon left unexplained, and no plan names. Just the method.
lines.say: No jargon left unexplained, and no plan names. Just the method.

lines.text: Chapter one: the four words that decide your bill.
lines.say: Chapter one: the four words that decide your bill.

lines.text: Every plan, from your job or from the marketplace, is built from the same four parts.
lines.say: Every plan, from your job or from the marketplace, is built from the same four parts.

lines.text: First, the premium. That's what you pay every month just to have the plan, even if you never use it.
lines.say: First, the premium. That's what you pay every month just to have the plan, even if you never use it.

lines.text: Second, the deductible. That's how much of your care you pay yourself before the plan starts sharing the cost.
lines.say: Second, the deductible. That's how much of your care you pay yourself before the plan starts sharing the cost.

lines.text: For single coverage, the average deductible was $1,886 in 2025, among plans that have one.
lines.say: For single coverage, the average deductible was one thousand eight hundred eighty-six dollars in twenty twenty-five, among plans that have one.

scene.label: Avg single deductible, 2025
scene.sub: KFF, plans with a general deductible

lines.text: Third, copays and coinsurance. A copay is a flat fee, like $30 for a visit. Coinsurance is a percentage, like 20% of the bill.
lines.say: Third, copays and coinsurance. A copay is a flat fee, like thirty dollars for a visit. Coinsurance is a percentage, like twenty percent of the bill.

lines.text: Fourth, and most important, the out-of-pocket maximum.
lines.say: Fourth, and most important, the out-of-pocket maximum.

scene.title: Fourth, and most important, the out-of-pocket ma

lines.text: It's the most you can pay for covered, in-network care in a year. After that, the plan pays 100%.
lines.say: It's the most you can pay for covered, in-network care in a year. After that, the plan pays a hundred percent.

lines.text: Premiums don't count toward it. Deductibles, copays and coinsurance do.
lines.say: Premiums don't count toward it. Deductibles, copays and coinsurance do.

lines.text: And the legal ceiling keeps climbing. For marketplace and most job plans, the cap is $12,000 for one person in 2027.
lines.say: And the legal ceiling keeps climbing. For marketplace and most job plans, the cap is twelve thousand dollars for one person in twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: That's up from $6,350 in 2014, and $24,000 for a family in 2027.
lines.say: That's up from six thousand three hundred fifty dollars in twenty fourteen, and twenty-four thousand for a family in twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: Your own plan's max is usually lower than the legal ceiling, so look for the real number on the plan summary.
lines.say: Your own plan's max is usually lower than the legal ceiling, so look for the real number on the plan summary.

lines.text: Every plan has to give you a standard Summary of Benefits and Coverage, so the numbers sit in the same places on each one.
lines.say: Every plan has to give you a standard Summary of Benefits and Coverage, so the numbers sit in the same places on each one.

lines.text: So here's the key idea. Your true yearly cost is premiums plus whatever you pay for care.
lines.say: So here's the key idea. Your true yearly cost is premiums plus whatever you pay for care.

lines.text: The premium is guaranteed. Everything else depends on how your year goes.
lines.say: The premium is guaranteed. Everything else depends on how your year goes.

lines.text: Chapter two: guess your year, then check your doctors.
lines.say: Chapter two: guess your year, then check your doctors.

lines.text: Step one is an honest guess about next year.
lines.say: Step one is an honest guess about next year.

lines.text: Look at last year. How many doctor visits, prescriptions, or tests did you actually have?
lines.say: Look at last year. How many doctor visits, prescriptions, or tests did you actually have?

lines.text: Then add what you already know is coming: a baby, a surgery, therapy, braces, a new prescription.
lines.say: Then add what you already know is coming: a baby, a surgery, therapy, braces, a new prescription.

lines.text: Sort yourself into a light year, a medium year, or a heavy year. You'll use that in the math.
lines.say: Sort yourself into a light year, a medium year, or a heavy year. You'll use that in the math.

lines.text: One bit of good news: most plans must cover in-network preventive care, like a yearly checkup and many vaccines, at no cost to you.
lines.say: One bit of good news: most plans must cover in-network preventive care, like a yearly checkup and many vaccines, at no cost to you.

scene.label: In-network preventive care
scene.sub: required for most plans under the ACA

lines.text: So a checkup alone doesn't make a year medium. Count the care beyond that.
lines.say: So a checkup alone doesn't make a year medium. Count the care beyond that.

lines.text: Step two: check that your doctors and your drugs are covered.
lines.say: Step two: check that your doctors and your drugs are covered.

lines.text: This is where the plan type matters. There are four common ones.
lines.say: This is where the plan type matters. There are four common ones.

lines.text: An HMO covers only its network, and usually needs a referral to see a specialist.
lines.say: An HMO covers only its network, and usually needs a referral to see a specialist.

lines.text: A PPO also pays something outside the network, at a higher cost to you, and usually needs no referral.
lines.say: A PPO also pays something outside the network, at a higher cost to you, and usually needs no referral.

lines.text: An EPO is network-only like an HMO, but usually without referrals.
lines.say: An EPO is network-only like an HMO, but usually without referrals.

lines.text: And an HDHP is a high-deductible plan that can come with a health savings account. More on that soon.
lines.say: And an HDHP is a high-deductible plan that can come with a health savings account. More on that soon.

lines.text: Whatever the type, search the plan's own directory for your doctors, and call the office to confirm.
lines.say: Whatever the type, search the plan's own directory for your doctors, and call the office to confirm.

lines.text: Then look up each prescription in the plan's drug list, called a formulary, and note its tier.
lines.say: Then look up each prescription in the plan's drug list, called a formulary, and note its tier.

lines.text: Out-of-network care usually doesn't count toward the in-network max, so one wrong doctor can blow up the math.
lines.say: Out-of-network care usually doesn't count toward the in-network max, so one wrong doctor can blow up the math.

lines.text: Chapter three: the total-cost math.
lines.say: Chapter three: the total-cost math.

lines.text: Step three is where most people skip ahead, and where the real money is.
lines.say: Step three is where most people skip ahead, and where the real money is.

lines.text: Let's compare two made-up job plans for one person. We'll keep it simple and skip copays.
lines.say: Let's compare two made-up job plans for one person. We'll keep it simple and skip copays.

lines.text: Plan A costs $150 a month. It has a $1,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $4,000 max.
lines.say: Plan A costs a hundred fifty dollars a month. It has a one thousand dollar deductible, twenty percent coinsurance, and a four thousand dollar max.

lines.text: Plan B costs $50 a month. It has a $3,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, a $6,000 max, and the employer puts $500 in a health savings account.
lines.say: Plan B costs fifty dollars a month. It has a three thousand dollar deductible, twenty percent coinsurance, a six thousand dollar max, and the employer puts five hundred dollars in a health savings account.

lines.text: A year of premiums is $1,800 for Plan A and $600 for Plan B.
lines.say: A year of premiums is eighteen hundred dollars for Plan A and six hundred for Plan B.

lines.text: Now run three years: light, medium, and heavy.
lines.say: Now run three years: light, medium, and heavy.

lines.text: Light year, $500 of care. Plan A: $1,800 plus $500 is $2,300.
lines.say: Light year, five hundred dollars of care. Plan A: eighteen hundred plus five hundred is twenty-three hundred dollars.

lines.text: Plan B: $600 plus $500, minus the $500 from the employer, is $600.
lines.say: Plan B: six hundred plus five hundred, minus the five hundred from the employer, is six hundred dollars.

lines.text: In a light year, Plan B wins by $1,700.
lines.say: In a light year, Plan B wins by seventeen hundred dollars.

lines.text: Medium year, $5,000 of care. Plan A: the $1,000 deductible, plus 20% of the other $4,000, is $1,800.
lines.say: Medium year, five thousand dollars of care. Plan A: the one thousand dollar deductible, plus twenty percent of the other four thousand, is eighteen hundred.

lines.text: Add $1,800 of premiums and Plan A costs $3,600.
lines.say: Add eighteen hundred of premiums and Plan A costs thirty-six hundred dollars.

lines.text: Plan B: the $3,000 deductible, plus 20% of $2,000, is $3,400.
lines.say: Plan B: the three thousand dollar deductible, plus twenty percent of two thousand, is thirty-four hundred.

lines.text: Add $600 of premiums, subtract the $500 from the employer, and Plan B costs $3,500.
lines.say: Add six hundred of premiums, subtract the five hundred from the employer, and Plan B costs thirty-five hundred.

lines.text: That's nearly a tie. Plan B is just $100 cheaper.
lines.say: That's nearly a tie. Plan B is just a hundred dollars cheaper.

lines.text: Heavy year, $40,000 of care, like a surgery. Both plans hit their out-of-pocket max.
lines.say: Heavy year, forty thousand dollars of care, like a surgery. Both plans hit their out-of-pocket max.

lines.text: Plan A: $1,800 of premiums plus the $4,000 max is $5,800.
lines.say: Plan A: eighteen hundred of premiums plus the four thousand dollar max is fifty-eight hundred dollars.

lines.text: Plan B: $600 plus the $6,000 max, minus $500, is $6,100.
lines.say: Plan B: six hundred plus the six thousand dollar max, minus five hundred, is sixty-one hundred dollars.

lines.text: So in a heavy year, Plan A wins, but only by $300.
lines.say: So in a heavy year, Plan A wins, but only by three hundred dollars.

lines.text: Put the three years side by side and the picture is clear.
lines.say: Put the three years side by side and the picture is clear.

lines.text: In this example, the low-premium plan wins most years, and loses the worst year by a little.
lines.say: In this example, the low-premium plan wins most years, and loses the worst year by a little.

lines.text: But that flips with different numbers, so run your own plans through the same three years.
lines.say: But that flips with different numbers, so run your own plans through the same three years.

lines.text: There's also a quick worst-case check: a year of premiums plus the out-of-pocket max.
lines.say: There's also a quick worst-case check: a year of premiums plus the out-of-pocket max.

lines.text: For Plan A that's $5,800. For Plan B it's $6,100 after the employer's $500. That's your ceiling for covered in-network care.
lines.say: For Plan A that's fifty-eight hundred dollars. For Plan B it's sixty-one hundred after the employer's five hundred. That's your ceiling for covered in-network care.

lines.text: The one question to ask: can you cover the higher deductible if the bad year happens in January?
lines.say: The one question to ask: can you cover the higher deductible if the bad year happens in January?

scene.label: Can you cover it?
scene.sub: Plan B's deductible, due before sharing starts

lines.text: Chapter four: the tax accounts.
lines.say: Chapter four: the tax accounts.

lines.text: Step four: use the accounts that let you pay for care with untaxed money.
lines.say: Step four: use the accounts that let you pay for care with untaxed money.

lines.text: The big one is the health savings account, or HSA, which you can open when you're on an eligible high-deductible plan.
lines.say: The big one is the health savings account, or H S A, which you can open when you're on an eligible high-deductible plan.

lines.text: For 2027, you can put in up to $4,500 for yourself, or $9,000 for a family.
lines.say: For twenty twenty-seven, you can put in up to forty-five hundred dollars for yourself, or nine thousand for a family.

lines.text: If you're 55 or older, you can add another $1,000.
lines.say: If you're fifty-five or older, you can add another thousand dollars.

lines.text: To qualify in 2027, a job plan's deductible must be at least $1,750 for one person, or $3,500 for a family.
lines.say: To qualify in twenty twenty-seven, a job plan's deductible must be at least seventeen hundred fifty dollars for one person, or thirty-five hundred for a family.

lines.text: Money goes in before income tax, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free for qualified medical costs.
lines.say: Money goes in before income tax, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free for qualified medical costs.

lines.text: For example, putting in $1,000 in the 22% tax bracket cuts your federal income tax by $220.
lines.say: For example, putting in a thousand dollars in the twenty-two percent tax bracket cuts your federal income tax by two hundred twenty dollars.

lines.text: Through payroll, it usually skips Social Security and Medicare taxes too.
lines.say: Through payroll, it usually skips Social Security and Medicare taxes too.

lines.text: And unlike an FSA, the money is yours. It rolls over and stays with you if you change jobs.
lines.say: And unlike an FSA, the money is yours. It rolls over and stays with you if you change jobs.

scene.label: Your HSA
scene.sub: it stays with you between jobs

lines.text: There's also a newer twist. Since 2026, bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans count as HSA-eligible.
lines.say: There's also a newer twist. Since twenty twenty-six, bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans count as H S A eligible.

scene.headline: Marketplace bronze and catastrophic plans now HSA-eligible
scene.source: One Big Beautiful Bill Act; IRS Notice 2026-05

lines.text: If you can't use an HSA, a job's flexible spending account, or FSA, also uses pre-tax money.
lines.say: If you can't use an H S A, a job's flexible spending account, or F S A, also uses pre-tax money.

lines.text: The limit was $3,400 for 2026 and usually rises a little each year, but most of it is use-it-or-lose-it, so only put in what you're sure to spend.
lines.say: The limit was thirty-four hundred dollars for twenty twenty-six and usually rises a little each year, but most of it is use-it-or-lose-it, so only put in what you're sure to spend.

scene.label: Health FSA limit, 2026
scene.sub: some plans allow a carryover or grace period

lines.text: Buying on the marketplace instead? Then the plans come in metal tiers.
lines.say: Buying on the marketplace instead? Then the plans come in metal tiers.

lines.text: The percent is roughly the share of typical costs the plan pays. Lower tiers mean lower premiums and higher costs when you use care.
lines.say: The percent is roughly the share of typical costs the plan pays. Lower tiers mean lower premiums and higher costs when you use care.

lines.text: If your income qualifies for cost-sharing reductions, you only get them on a silver plan. They lower your deductible, copays and max.
lines.say: If your income qualifies for cost-sharing reductions, you only get them on a silver plan. They lower your deductible, copays and max.

lines.text: And subsidies changed. The enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025.
lines.say: And subsidies changed. The enhanced premium tax credits expired at the end of twenty twenty-five.

scene.headline: Enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired Dec 31, 2025

lines.text: That brought back the cliff: above 400% of the poverty level, there's no premium tax credit.
lines.say: That brought back the cliff: above four hundred percent of the poverty level, there's no premium tax credit.

lines.text: When this video was made, in fall 2026, a House-passed bill to restore the enhanced credits had not become law, so check your own estimate on HealthCare.gov.
lines.say: When this video was made, in fall twenty twenty-six, a House-passed bill to restore the enhanced credits had not become law, so check your own estimate on HealthCare dot gov.

lines.text: Chapter five: deadlines and common mistakes.
lines.say: Chapter five: deadlines and common mistakes.

lines.text: On HealthCare.gov, open enrollment for 2027 opened November 1, 2026 and runs through January 15, 2027.
lines.say: On HealthCare dot gov, open enrollment for twenty twenty-seven opened November first, twenty twenty-six and runs through January fifteenth, twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: Pick by December 15 to be covered from January 1.
lines.say: Pick by December fifteenth to be covered from January first.

lines.text: Some state marketplaces use different dates, and job plans set their own window, often just a couple of weeks.
lines.say: Some state marketplaces use different dates, and job plans set their own window, often just a couple of weeks.

lines.text: Miss it, and you usually wait a year unless you have a qualifying life event, like a move, a birth, or losing other coverage.
lines.say: Miss it, and you usually wait a year unless you have a qualifying life event, like a move, a birth, or losing other coverage.

lines.text: Now the mistakes. Mistake one: auto-renewing without looking. Premiums, networks, and drug lists change every year.
lines.say: Now the mistakes. Mistake one: auto-renewing without looking. Premiums, networks, and drug lists change every year.

lines.text: Mistake two: comparing only premiums, which is the trap from the start of this video.
lines.say: Mistake two: comparing only premiums, which is the trap from the start of this video.

lines.text: Mistake three: not checking that your doctors and your drugs are in network.
lines.say: Mistake three: not checking that your doctors and your drugs are in network.

lines.text: Mistake four: ignoring the employer's HSA deposit, which can cover part of the deductible.
lines.say: Mistake four: ignoring the employer's HSA deposit, which can cover part of the deductible.

lines.text: And one more for couples: compare both employers' plans, including the cost of covering a spouse.
lines.say: And one more for couples: compare both employers' plans, including the cost of covering a spouse.

lines.text: Here's the whole thing on one screen.
lines.say: Here's the whole thing on one screen.

lines.text: Chapter six: the recap.
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Your real cost is premiums plus your share of care, capped by the out-of-pocket max.
lines.say: Your real cost is premiums plus your share of care, capped by the out-of-pocket max.

lines.text: In our example, the cheaper premium won the light and medium years, by $1,700 and $100.
lines.say: In our example, the cheaper premium won the light and medium years, by seventeen hundred dollars and by just a hundred.

lines.text: And it lost the heavy year by just $300.
lines.say: And it lost the heavy year by just three hundred dollars.

lines.text: Your numbers will differ, but the method doesn't: three years, one total, and the deadline on your calendar.
lines.say: Your numbers will differ, but the method doesn't: three years, one total, and the deadline on your calendar.

post.yt_desc:
Most people compare health plans by the monthly premium, but your real yearly cost is premiums plus your share of care, capped by the out-of-pocket maximum. This guide explains premiums, deductibles, coinsurance and out-of-pocket maximums, then runs two example plans through a light, medium and heavy year with exact math. It also covers 2027 HSA limits, the 2026 FSA limit, marketplace metal tiers, the subsidy changes since 2026, and the 2027 open enrollment dates.

CHAPTERS

Sources: KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey (Oct 2025); IRS Rev. Proc. 2026-24 (May 2026) and Notice 2026-05; CMS 2027 Notice of Benefit and Payment Parameters (May 2026); HealthCare.gov open enrollment dates (CMS, Aug 2026); KFF and CNBC on ACA premium tax credits (Jan 2026).

News and education, not financial advice.
